title: Performance of a Hot Rb Vapour-Based Portable Quantum Memory
authors: Kenneth Gregory, Konrad Socha, Khaled Mnaymneh, Connor Kupchak
abstract: Quantum repeaters will be paramount to the success of the future quantum internet. Presently however, the losses incurred in fibre communications are unsustainable when fragile quantum states are transmitted over long distances. The most effective repeater nodes will require incorporation of a minimum of two quantum memory units (QMems) for successful operation. Therefore a network composed of numerous nodes will ideally require scalable repeaters that contain QMems that are portable, robust and do not require a high amount of overhead. Here we investigate the performance of a commercial QMem based on a warm vapour of Rb atoms. Specifically, we characterize the coherence time, absolute efficiency, signal to noise ratio and bit error ratio of this device over a range of vapour temperatures that are readily controllable. For our system, we place these performance metrics into the same conventions as those established for current optical communication protocols. Development of QMem systems meeting these benchmarks will be a vital step for seamless integration of QMems systems into present-day communication architectures.
summary: This paper experimentally characterizes a portable quantum memory based on warm rubidium vapour, designed for use in quantum repeaters. The authors measure key performance indicators like coherence time, efficiency, SNR, and BER across varying temperatures. The results demonstrate that the device meets several classical communication benchmarks, marking a vital step toward integrating quantum memories into real-world quantum communication architectures.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop portable, robust, and scalable Quantum Memory (QMem) units necessary for building functional quantum repeaters to overcome signal loss in long-distance quantum communication networks.
main_result: The study successfully characterized the QMem performance, demonstrating that the system achieves SNR and BER values meeting classical telecommunication benchmarks under optimal conditions (e.g., 90°C, 5 $\mu$s storage time).
method: Performance metrics like coherence time, absolute efficiency, SNR, and BER were characterized by measuring the storage and retrieval of quantum states using a warm Rb vapour cell.
model_or_system: The system utilizes a commercial QMem based on a warm rubidium (Rb) vapour cell, operating via Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) on the D1 transition of Rb atoms.
key_observables: Coherence time, absolute efficiency ($\eta$), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and Bit Error Ratio (BER).
important_parameters: Vapour temperature (60°C - 90°C), storage time (up to 100 $\mu$s), and the EIT regime.
main_assumptions: It is assumed that the classical offset observed at long storage times is due to ground state decoherence and can be accurately subtracted for coherence time fitting.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup schematic, sample retrieved pulses, storage efficiency decay vs. time/temperature, and the dependence of SNR and BER on temperature and storage time.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first detailing the setup and measuring fundamental metrics like efficiency and coherence time. It then extends the analysis to calculate and report SNR and BER, comparing these results against established classical communication standards to assess quantum network viability.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware bottleneck for quantum networking by providing empirical data on a solid-state, scalable quantum memory platform, which is crucial for quantum information scientists.

The probe beam is detuned from the control field by the 87Rb ground state splitting frequency using an electro-optical modulator (EOM). Both fields are coupled into separate input fibre ports of the QMem system.
